title: [A2 • Band 4.0] Bài 109: The Saffron Crocus: The Golden Spice
passageHtml:
PASSAGE 109 (LEVEL A2 • BAND 4.0)

The Saffron Crocus: The Golden Spice

Paragraph 1. Saffron comes from the red threads of a small purple flower called Crocus sativus. People call it 'vegetable gold' because it is the most expensive spice in the world. For more than three thousand years, cooks and doctors across three continents have used saffron. Unlike wild flowers, this saffron plant cannot make seeds or grow alone in nature. To grow new plants, farmers must dig up and divide its round underground bulbs called corms.

Paragraph 2. Saffron costs a lot of money because picking the flowers is very hard work. Each flower blooms for only two or three weeks in late autumn. The flowers open early in the morning and die quickly in warm air. Workers must pick every flower by hand before sunrise, because strong midday heat spoils the plant's fine smell. To make one kilogram of dry saffron, pickers must gather between 150,000 and 200,000 blossoms.

Paragraph 3. Old wall paintings found on the Greek island of Santorini show young women collecting saffron flowers in woven baskets. In ancient Rome, people put sweet-smelling saffron water in public baths and threw it on theatre floors. Rich Roman brides also wore bright yellow wedding veils dyed with saffron.

Paragraph 4. In the Middle Ages, saffron cost more than gold, so dishonest sellers often cheated buyers by mixing it with honey, oil, or cheap petals. German towns created strict laws and punished cheaters severely. Even today, machines cannot pick the delicate flowers, so workers must still harvest every crop by hand. Currently, Iran produces over eighty-five percent of the world's saffron, though irregular rain and late frosts threaten future harvests.
